title: Effects of Oil Supply Disruptions on Oil Exporters, Importers - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed study of past OPEC-identified oil supply shocks finds both Canada (net exporter) and the euro area (net importer) suffered lower industrial production and higher inflation (~0.2-0.25 pp per 10% oil rise). Because oil extraction is a small GDP share (5% in Canada, ~1% in the U.S.), the authors argue the U.S. net-exporter status will not make it a net winner from current oil disruptions.

themes.theme: Exporter status is no oil-shock shield

insights.claim: Historical oil supply disruptions slowed growth and raised inflation in both Canada (a large net oil exporter) and the euro area (a large net oil importer), with effects not significantly different across the two.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Being a net oil exporter does not insulate a developed economy from stagflationary oil supply shocks.
insights.quote: Our results for Canada and the euro area suggest that the economic effects of past oil supply disruptions are not significantly different across the two economies.

insights.claim: Because U.S. oil and gas extraction is only about 1% of GDP, the U.S. shift to net oil exporter status in late 2018 likely does not make it a net beneficiary of oil supply disruptions; the sector gain will not offset broader economic damage.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Don't price U.S. growth as a winner from the current oil price spike; expect net drag plus inflation.
insights.quote: the combined U.S. oil and gas extraction sector represents a relatively small share of total output, only around 1% of GDP.
insights.locator: The United States became a net

insights.claim: Canada's oil extraction industry is only about 5% of GDP, too small to offset the costs higher oil prices impose on the rest of its economy, despite some positive wealth effects.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Energy-sector share of GDP, not net-export status, governs whether an economy wins from oil shocks.
insights.quote: the oil extraction industry in Canada only represents about 5% of its GDP

insights.claim: Oil windfall gains in exporters are blunted because profits often accrue to foreign shareholders and may be saved rather than spent, weakening the domestic wealth effect.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Ownership structure of the energy sector matters for how much of an oil windfall reaches domestic demand.
insights.quote: Gains from higher oil prices often accrue to foreign shareholders and might be saved, blunting the wealth effects.

insights.claim: Canada's tight integration with the U.S. means an oil shock that depresses U.S. output spills over to Canadian aggregate demand, offsetting exporter gains.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Trade-partner exposure can turn an oil exporter into a net loser; watch U.S. demand for Canadian outlook.
insights.quote: the effects of an oil shock in the U.S. economy can spill over and further depress aggregate demand in Canada

insights.claim: A supply-driven 10% real oil price increase lowers euro area industrial production by up to 1% over the first year, with the decline persisting at longer horizons.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Euro area industrial activity is highly exposed to the current oil price rise; expect a persistent drag.
insights.quote: Industrial production declines steadily over the first year by up to 1% in response to a 10% increase in oil prices

insights.claim: In Canada, industrial production barely responds in the first year after an adverse oil supply shock but falls by up to 0.5% at longer horizons, implying a delayed hit for exporters.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Exporter damage shows up with a lag; early resilience can mislead.
insights.quote: In Canada, the response of industrial production is close to zero in the first year after the shock and falls by up to 0.5% at longer horizons.

insights.claim: Oil supply news shocks raise the unemployment rate after about six months in both Canada and the euro area.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Labor-market deterioration from an oil shock appears roughly two quarters out.
insights.quote: oil supply news shocks lead to an increase in the unemployment rate after the first six months in both Canada and the euro area

insights.claim: In Canada, mining and oil and gas extraction output rises up to 1% (1981-2007 sample) and about 0.5% (1997-2019) after an oil supply shock, while non-energy manufacturing declines, especially in the earlier sample.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Sector rotation within exporters: energy up, manufacturing down; the energy boost has shrunk in recent decades.
insights.locator: We find that the energy-related sectors

insights.claim: Unlike Canada, the euro area sees production drop in manufacturing, electricity supply, and mining and quarrying alike after an adverse oil supply shock.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: For importers there is no sectoral offset; the hit is broad-based.

insights.claim: A supply disruption raising oil prices 10% on impact lifts headline inflation by about 0.18 pp in Canada, 0.25 pp in the euro area, and about 0.3 pp in the United States, with peaks within 12 months.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Rule of thumb: roughly 0.2-0.3 pp headline CPI per 10% supply-driven oil rise, front-loaded in the first year.
insights.quote: is associated with a 0.18 percentage point increase in headline inflation in Canada and a 0.25 percentage point increase in the euro area
insights.locator: We next turn to the responses

insights.claim: Oil prices rise significantly after an oil supply news shock and the increase persists for more than 24 months.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Supply-driven oil spikes are not quickly reversed; plan for a multi-year elevated price path.
insights.quote: oil prices increase significantly after an oil supply news shock, and the increase persists for more than 24 months.

insights.claim: The economic effect of higher oil prices depends on the source: supply shocks produce stagflation globally, whereas demand-driven price rises can lift even oil importers via stronger export demand.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Diagnose whether the current oil rally is supply- or demand-driven before positioning on growth.
insights.quote: if an increase in global demand is the source of rising oil prices, oil-importing economies can also see positive growth
insights.locator: Oil price changes from supply shocks

insights.claim: Adverse oil supply shocks can trigger a negative feedback loop in which central banks tighten to fight inflation, raising borrowing costs and further depressing aggregate demand.
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: Central bank reaction to oil-driven inflation can amplify the growth hit; rates exposure matters.
insights.quote: a central bank may tighten monetary policy and raise interest rates to lower inflation, which increases borrowing costs and further depresses aggregate demand
insights.locator: Oil price changes from supply shocks

insights.claim: Oil supply news shocks can be identified from oil futures price moves in a one-day window around OPEC production announcements, since demand news is already priced beforehand (Känzig 2021 method).
insights.speaker: Wataru Miyamoto
insights.so_what: OPEC-announcement-day futures moves are a clean, tradable signal of supply news.
